issues.legal_issue: A mining lease extension correcting an initially shortened lease term could not be set aside solely because an auction might yield higher revenue to the State.
material_facts: The State policy contemplated leases for newly identified mining areas for a term normally between three and five years.
The lease was initially granted for one year even though the Collector considered that it should have been granted for at least three years.
The Collector extended the lease by two years to correct the short initial term.
The State set aside the extension, relying mainly on its decision to auction the mining rights to obtain higher revenue.
issues.conclusion: The State was not justified in setting aside the extension on the ground that an auction could produce higher revenue; the extension was consistent with the State's policy and the lease terms.
issues.legal_principle: A State obligation incurred in accordance with its own policy must be enforced; the possibility of earning somewhat higher revenue through an auction, by itself, is not a ground to avoid that obligation. The Court relied on the State policy and the stipulations of the mining lease and cited no statutory provision or earlier case for this point.

predicates.challenge_to_setting_aside_of_mining_lea: A party challenged the setting aside of an extension to a mining lease.
predicates.policy_contemplated_a_minimum_lease_term: The State's policy contemplated a lease term longer than the initial term granted.
predicates.extension_corrected_initially_shortened_: The authority extended the lease to make up for an initial term that was shorter than the policy contemplated.
predicates.state_interference_based_on_higher_aucti: The State set aside the extension because an auction was expected to produce higher revenue.
predicates.state_interference_unjustified: The State's setting aside of the extension was not justified.

issues.definition: When a challenged interference with a mining lease extension corrects an initially shortened term contemplated by policy, higher expected auction revenue alone does not justify the interference.

issues.legal_issue: A claimant entitled to relief should not be denied effective relief solely because proceedings consumed time when the delay was not the claimant's fault and no intervening circumstance made relief inequitable or impossible.
material_facts: The appellant pursued legal proceedings, and the delay in their final resolution was not attributable to him.
No auction had taken place and no third-party interest had been created in the mining rights.
The mine remained unoperated during the time the appellant's operation fell short of the three-year term.
The State's intervening order stopping the operation was found unsustainable.
The appellant sought to operate the mine for the balance needed to receive the benefit of the full term, with credit for time already operated.
issues.conclusion: The appellant was entitled to effective relief and was to be allowed to operate the mine for the balance of the three-year term, subject to adjustment for the time already operated and payment under the lease.
issues.legal_principle: Ordinarily, relief is assessed by reference to the claimant's position when litigation began, and a successful claimant should, as far as possible, be put in the position they would have occupied absent the wrong. Later events may justify withholding relief if they make it redundant, impossible, or inequitable, including through third-party interests or a changed balance of equities; relief should not be denied solely for time lost in proceedings when the claimant was not at fault. The Court cited no statutory provision or earlier case for this principle.
issues.definition: This rule means that a claimant receives effective relief when the claimant was entitled to relief, did not cause the litigation delay, and no intervening circumstance makes relief inequitable or impossible.
